title: Chelow
subtitle: Persian steamed basmati rice with tahdig crust
excerpt: Chelow is the Iranian method for cooking basmati rice: parboiled, drained, then steamed over low heat with oil and a little water so the base forms a golden crust called tahdig. The crust is the prized part of the dish and the one thing every Persian cook is judged on.
sourceNotes: Margaret Shaida, The Legendary Cuisine of Persia (1992). Chelow and the tahdig method described in detail as the foundation of all Persian rice dishes. Najmieh Batmanglij, Food of Life: Ancient Persian and Modern Iranian Cooking and Ceremonies (1986). The two-stage cooking method, wrapping the lid in a cloth, and tahdig variations documented comprehensively.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Chelow is best served immediately. The tahdig crust loses its crispness as it cools.

content.text: Chelow is the Persian method of cooking rice: the grains are parboiled until just tender, drained, then returned to the pot with a little oil and steamed over low heat until a golden, crispy crust forms at the base. That crust, called tahdig, is the reason chelow is more than just rice. Getting it right takes attention to heat and timing, but it is learnable with a single session.

items.prepNote: rinsed three times until the water runs clear
optional, added to the finished rice
ground, dissolved in 2 tbsp hot water

content.text: A heavy-based saucepan with a tight-fitting lid is essential. Wrap the lid in a clean tea towel before placing it on the pan: this absorbs the steam and keeps it inside so the grains steam dry rather than turning wet and sticky. The cloth must be pulled well away from the heat source.

Bring a large pot of water to the boil and add {{sea-salt-fine}}. Add the rinsed {{basmati-rice}} and stir once. Parboil for six to seven minutes: the grains should be tender on the outside but still have a chalky white core when you bite one. Drain immediately into a large colander.

Return the empty saucepan to the hob over a medium-high heat. Add {{sunflower-oil}} and 3 tablespoons of water. When the oil is hot and shimmering, add a thin layer of drained rice to cover the base completely, pressing it down gently.
Add the remaining rice in a mound on top, not pressing it down. If using {{saffron}}, drizzle the dissolved saffron water over the top of the rice mound.
Wrap the lid tightly in a clean tea towel, tying or holding the ends safely away from the heat. Place the wrapped lid firmly on the pot.

Cook over medium-high heat for three minutes until steam builds, then reduce to the lowest possible heat and cook for 30 to 35 minutes. The base should be golden and crispy. Resist lifting the lid early.
Take the pan off the heat and place it on a cold, wet cloth or in a shallow tray of cold water for two minutes. This helps the tahdig release from the base. Remove the lid.

Spoon the fluffy top rice onto a platter. Then invert the pan over the platter so the golden tahdig crust comes out whole in one piece. If using {{unsalted-butter}}, dot it over the steamed rice to melt.

items.symptom: The tahdig is burned, not golden
items.cause: Heat too high during the steaming phase
items.fix: The low steam phase must be the lowest your hob can go. Use a heat diffuser if available. Check at 25 minutes next time.

items.symptom: The tahdig is pale and not crispy
items.cause: Not enough heat at the start, or not enough oil
items.fix: The oil must be hot before the rice goes in for the crust to form. Start at medium-high for three minutes, then drop to the lowest heat.

items.symptom: The rice is sticky and clumped
items.cause: Not rinsed enough before cooking, or parboiled too long
items.fix: Rinse until the water runs clear. Parboil for no more than seven minutes: the grains should still have a chalky core when drained.

items.symptom: The tahdig comes out in pieces, not whole
items.cause: Rested for too short a time on the cold cloth
items.fix: Two minutes on a cold, wet surface lets the crust contract from the pan. If it still sticks, chisel it out carefully: the flavour is the same.

content.text: Rice is the centrepiece of the Iranian meal and chelow is its purest expression. The word chelow refers specifically to plain steamed rice with tahdig, as opposed to polow, which is rice cooked with other ingredients. At a Persian dinner table, chelow is served alongside khoresh (stew), kebab, or grilled meat. The tahdig is shared out among diners, with the crispest pieces going to honoured guests. Arguments about who got the most tahdig are a common family memory. The technique dates back centuries and is taught from parent to child: knowing how to make a good tahdig is a mark of competence in an Iranian kitchen.
